patch.title: Hardness limits for scheduling and network planning (unaudited)
patch.description: Hardness-of-approximation ceilings for the combinatorial problems behind constellation tasking, ground-station and gateway siting, routing, beam frequency assignment and network partitioning become formal claims awaiting outside checks rather than beliefs: beating Goemans-Williamson Max-Cut (beam two-colouring) or factor-2 vertex cover (minimal link/beam sets) is NP-hard given 102 (UGC claimed with an unaudited Lean proof, T3); uniform sparsest cut (mesh partitioning) has no constant-factor algorithm (conditional, T1); metric k-median siting is pinned at 1+2/e. These are worst-case ceilings for general graphs and metrics. Operational instances are geometric (toroidal +Grid/Motif laser meshes, Earth-surface siting, disk-like beam-conflict graphs), and there approximation schemes or O(1) algorithms exist, so the ceilings bound general-purpose solver research and vendor claims about general instances, not constellation planning.

patch.thesis: If research-grade AI math reaches outside engineers in 2027 (base case) and checking is cheap, on-demand analysis spreads through space engineering by 2028. New program schedules shrink about 20-30% (38% at most), since tests, factories and launches run on physical time.

Commercial operators fly new hardware qualified mainly by AI analysis around 2029-30 (base case, Medium); government and crewed programs wait for a rulebook (2029, Medium) and broader credit (2030, Low). Analysis runs 2-5x faster, but test stands hold qualification savings to about 10-20% in the base case (at least 15% by 2031 is Low).

If AI agents can draft specifications and machine-checked proofs for flight code, verified code gets 15-120x cheaper per line by 2028-29 and first flies on landers and constellations about 2029 (base case, Medium). Regulators accept proof-based plans around 2030 (Medium); engine, entry, launch-safety and crewed credit stay Low by 2031.

If AI can certify combustion, flow and materials models, engines could earn model-based reuse life from about 2029 and an AI-designed alloy could fly by 2031 (Low in the base case, Medium in Recursive). Engines stay test-paced: each failure mode costs a redesign and re-test.

If AI does the theory and inference behind missions, science return per dollar rises from archives by 2028, and satellite methane data get calibrated error bars (both Medium, base case). Launch dates hold: LISA still flies in 2035, and the Habitable Worlds Observatory moves at budget pace.

patch.reader_hook: An AI agent formalized a Vlasov-Maxwell-Landau plasma result in 10 days for about $200, with no human-written code (one mathematician, 229 prompts). Two of its three failure modes, hypothesis creep and definition-alignment bugs, came from stating the problem. Only 16 partial-differential-equation and 12 dynamics families sit among the release's 372, reflecting which problems the lab chose to pose and which survived its filter.

patch.thesis: If AI settles famous fluid problems, up to unforced Navier–Stokes, the theorems change almost no engine, heat shield or orbit. Engineers get the proof machinery and on-demand error bars as verification evidence from about 2028 (base case), and math stops being a bottleneck around 2029.
